before.value: For active case work, routine data entry should feel immediate; basic searches or lookups should return in a couple of seconds at most, and anything beyond about three seconds for common actions is too slow. Routine entry and common lookups should stay very fast, ideally within a second or two, and saves and searches really shouldn’t drift past about three seconds in normal conditions. If something takes longer, the system should show a clear progress indicator and let the user know it’s still working rather than appearing frozen. If it goes beyond a reasonable threshold, it should fail gracefully, preserve what the user already entered, and offer a retry instead of making them start over. If a search, save, or common lookup is still running after the progress indicator has been up for a while, the system should time out based on the kind of action, but not so quickly that it cuts off normal outbreak work. The timeout should depend on how critical and how common the action is, with routine lookups timing out sooner than larger searches, imports, or cross-record checks. If the user is actively entering data, the system should be more patient in the background, but it still needs to stop waiting at some point and tell them clearly what failed. For outbreak-wide reporting or a large deduplication job, it should wait longer and use a different failure path, since those can be resumed or rerun without blocking immediate case work.

after.value: Timeout windows should be based on how often the action is used, how urgently the user needs the result to continue, and whether the work can safely continue in the background. Routine lookups should have short windows because they’re expected to return right away, active data-entry tasks should allow a bit more time so investigators aren’t interrupted in the middle of work, and larger outbreak-wide jobs should have the longest window and be handled more like background processing with status updates instead of making the user wait on the screen.

before.value: Connect related entities and events; preserve the core public health workflow so staff can review a signal, assign investigation ownership, document case and contact details, and record actions taken, while centralizing and making more consistent the linking of entities; treat lab reports, case reports, and referrals as related but distinct sources, and allow multiple sources to attach to the same investigation without losing original details. Use a single shared case record with linked entities underneath it so everyone works from the same source of truth; attribute each person's actions, notes, and status changes to their user account and timestamp them; prevent duplicate contacts or exposures by matching on identifiers and let staff merge records when needed; keep conflicting updates in the audit trail and require an authorized reviewer to resolve them before reports are finalized. The shared case should hold the core investigation status and overall summary, while linked people, contacts, exposures, and actions can be edited separately when they belong to different parts of the investigation; editing should be limited to what the investigator's role and assignment allow; linked details such as identifying information, lab results, and sensitive interview notes may need to remain restricted to a smaller group for legal or public health reasons; if a linked record is used in multiple active workflows, edits should be controlled carefully to prevent one team from overwriting information another team still depends on.

before.value: Staff should be able to see the previous status, who made the change, when it happened, and a short reason or note explaining why. For merged or reclassified records, preserve the chain of what happened so investigators can understand the decision later. History should not be hidden, but it may be summarized for everyday users while remaining available in full to authorized staff. On conflicting batch imports or external feeds, the system should block automatic updates, preserve both versions for review, display conflicting fields side by side, indicate any more authoritative source if defined, and retain the original data for audit purposes even if a preference rule is allowed for clearly minor, one-sided conflicts. The system should keep both conflicting versions in the audit trail and require an authorized reviewer to resolve the conflict before reports are finalized. Offline access should be limited to only the cases and data the investigator already has permission to see, with sensitive fields tightly restricted. Investigators may draft notes and queue certain updates while offline, but anything that could overwrite someone else’s work must wait for sync and conflict checking after reconnecting. If the case changed while they were away, the system should preserve both the offline submission and the newer online version for reviewer reconciliation rather than silently replacing one with the other.

before.value: Urgent changes should be approved by a small set of authorized supervisors or system admins, with the approval captured in the audit trail. The change should take effect quickly, but the system should keep the prior version available so it can be rolled back right away if it disrupts active work or turns out to be wrong. If reversed, staff should be able to restore the previous state without losing the history of what happened or who approved it. When a linked person, contact, exposure, or action record is shared across more than one active workflow, the person actively assigned or checked out for an urgent task gets edit priority first; everyone else should see it read-only or work on a draft. If the record is high-risk for conflicting changes, it should be briefly locked or require supervisor approval before commit. If updates still collide, the system should keep both, flag the conflict immediately, and have a reviewer decide which version becomes operative. A shared record should be locked or require supervisor approval when the change affects case status, exposure classification, contact tracing assignments, or anything that could change who is notified or what public health action happens next; approval is also expected when the record is already being edited by someone else or when the user is trying to change restricted sensitive data. A time-critical containment update, such as a positive lab result or urgent isolation action, can bypass the lock if a qualified supervisor or designated responder forces the update, but the system must log exactly why and alert the other users.

after.value: During downtime, staff must still be able to capture new cases, contacts, exposures, and critical actions through temporary offline logging or paper/emergency forms, and there must be a clean handoff so those entries can later be entered back into the system without losing timestamps, ownership, or links between records. Offline records should preserve the original time the action happened, who performed it, and how it relates to the case or contact it belongs to; nothing should be re-dated to the time of entry unless explicitly noted as such, and each paper or offline record should carry a unique local identifier or reference so it can be matched back cleanly during reconciliation. If the system is recovering, read-only access to existing case details should also be available.

before.value: Connect related entities and events; preserve the core public health workflow so staff can review a signal, assign investigation ownership, document case and contact details, and record actions taken, while centralizing and making more consistent the linking of entities; treat lab reports, case reports, and referrals as related but distinct sources, and allow multiple sources to attach to the same investigation without losing original details. Use a single shared case record with linked entities underneath it so everyone works from the same source of truth; attribute each person's actions, notes, and status changes to their user account and timestamp them; prevent duplicate contacts or exposures by matching on identifiers and let staff merge records when needed; keep conflicting updates in the audit trail and require an authorized reviewer to resolve them before reports are finalized. The shared case should hold the core investigation status and overall summary, while linked people, contacts, exposures, and actions can be edited separately when they belong to different parts of the investigation; editing should be limited to what the investigator's role and assignment allow; linked details such as identifying information, lab results, and sensitive interview notes may need to remain restricted to a smaller group for legal or public health reasons; if a linked record is used in multiple active workflows, edits should be controlled carefully to prevent one team from overwriting information another team still depends on. Anything already committed to the database should not be rolled back just because a later save timed out; preserve unsaved changes, but if the underlying record was already submitted or linked by someone else, conflicting edits should be cleared or flagged for review before resubmitting; sensitive or system-generated fields should be refreshed from the saved record rather than restored from the user's old screen state.

before.value: Staff should be able to see the previous status, who made the change, when it happened, and a short reason or note explaining why. For merged or reclassified records, preserve the chain of what happened so investigators can understand the decision later. History should not be hidden, but it may be summarized for everyday users while remaining available in full to authorized staff. On conflicting batch imports or external feeds, the system should block automatic updates, preserve both versions for review, display conflicting fields side by side, indicate any more authoritative source if defined, and retain the original data for audit purposes even if a preference rule is allowed for clearly minor, one-sided conflicts. The system should keep both conflicting versions in the audit trail and require an authorized reviewer to resolve the conflict before reports are finalized. Offline access should be limited to only the cases and data the investigator already has permission to see, with sensitive fields tightly restricted. Investigators may draft notes and queue certain updates while offline, but anything that could overwrite someone else's work must wait for sync and conflict checking after reconnecting. If the case changed while they were away, the system should preserve both the offline submission and the newer online version for reviewer reconciliation rather than silently replacing one with the other. Anything that has already been committed to the database should not be rolled back just because a later save timed out; if the underlying record was already submitted or linked by someone else, conflicting edits should be cleared or flagged for review before resubmission, and sensitive or system-generated fields should be refreshed from the saved record rather than restored from the user's old screen state. Authoritative identity, status, timestamp, linkage, ownership, and audit-related values should be reloaded from the persisted record after a save timeout, including case status, assigned investigator, last updated time, linked contacts or labs, and system-set identifiers or flags; any staged change in that category should only replace the saved value after explicit user confirmation. Pending edits should be preserved, with out-of-date or conflicting parts selectively flagged for review; purely local notes or draft comments can stay as-is, while edits to shared fields like demographics, status, relationships, exposures, or specimen details should be highlighted for reconciliation. Local notes should stay intact, and shared field edits should be flagged for review; intervention narrative fields like free-text rationale or implementation comments can be treated like notes if they are purely descriptive and not driving workflow.

before.value: Access should be based on role, jurisdiction, and need to know, with the default being as narrow as possible for anything sensitive or restricted. If a record is tied to a specific investigation, only the assigned team and the people supporting that jurisdiction should be able to view or edit it, and notes with especially sensitive details should be even more limited. Access can be broadened only when it’s necessary for coordinated response or supervision, but things like protected informant details or highly sensitive annotations should stay tightly controlled unless there’s a clear public health need. For restricted linked records and especially sensitive notes during rapid intervention or containment, the practical rule is minimum necessary access to get the action done, not blanket access to the whole record. The intervention team should see only the specific details needed for that task, editing should stay with the assigned case team or a designated lead unless there’s an urgent operational reason to widen it, and access should return to the tighter normal level once the immediate action is complete.
